questions.q: In which department, by the Court's account, do many of the most highly regarded Alsace vineyard sites lie?
questions.exp: The Haut-Rhin is the southern department, higher on average and better sheltered by the Vosges, so it is drier and sunnier and holds many of the most highly regarded sites around Colmar, Riquewihr and Turckheim. The Bas-Rhin to the north lies lower, where the mountains lose height and give less protection.

questions.q: What name does the Court give the large, neutral oak casks that line Alsace cellars?
questions.exp: A foudre is a large, old oak cask, often oval in Alsace, that gives no oak flavour and lets the wine ferment and rest without masking its fruit; new barriques are rare in the region. The Court's Introductory column notes little or no new oak, and its Certified column asks for the cask's name.

questions.q: Hugel et Fils, one of the producers the Court names, is based in which walled Alsace village?
questions.exp: Hugel has made wine in Riquewihr since the seventeenth century and pressed for the legal definition of Vendanges Tardives and Sélection de Grains Nobles in 1984. Of the Court's other names, Trimbach is in Ribeauvillé, Domaine Weinbach in Kaysersberg below the Schlossberg, Zind-Humbrecht in Turckheim and Marcel Deiss in Bergheim.

questions.q: Baeckeoffe, pork, lamb and beef marinated overnight in white wine and slow-baked with potatoes in a sealed dish, is on the menu. Which Alsace wine is the natural partner?
questions.exp: A dry Riesling, often the wine the meat was marinated in, cuts the richness of the braise with its acidity and matches its savoury depth; dry Pinot Gris or Sylvaner work too. The Court's Alsace pairings are hearty and smoky: choucroute, Flammkuchen and cured meats such as bacon and sausages, which the region's dry whites carry well and its sweet late harvest wines do not.

questions.q: Which Alsace appellation does the Court name as an alternative, cost-effective source of traditional method sparkling wine?
questions.exp: Crémant d'Alsace, an appellation since 1976, is made by second fermentation in bottle, mostly from Pinot Blanc and Auxerrois with Chardonnay allowed and the rosé from Pinot Noir alone, and spends at least nine months on its lees. It is the second largest French sparkling appellation after Champagne and costs far less, which is the value case the Court's business row makes.

questions.q: Brand, one of the Court's example Alsace Grands Crus, rises above which town?
questions.exp: Brand is a steep granite Grand Cru above Turckheim, giving powerful Riesling and Pinot Gris. Of the Court's other examples, Schlossberg is the granite Riesling site at Kientzheim and Kaysersberg, first of the Grands Crus in 1975, and Hengst at Wintzenheim was one of the first two opened to Pinot Noir with the 2022 vintage; Thann is home to Rangen and Andlau to Kastelberg.

questions.q: By the Court's figure, Alsace wine made from white grape varieties accounts for more than what share of the region's output?
questions.exp: More than 90 per cent of Alsace wine is white, from Riesling, Pinot Gris, Gewurztraminer, Muscat, Pinot Blanc, Auxerrois and Silvaner, with Pinot Noir the one black grape for rosé, red and Crémant rosé. The Court gives the share in the same cell as the Vosges rain shadow that makes Alsace one of the driest and sunniest regions of France.
